opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about a lot. Some of our earlier work started from a simple observation: if you probe these models, you find they're building internal representations of the person they're talking to. Things like an estimate of the user's age, gender, education level, socioeconomic status. And that raised an obvious design question: what if you just showed that to the user? A kind of dashboard alongside the chat window that says, here's what the system currently seems to think about you.

The natural next step is to ask the same question about the model's representation of *itself*. What does the system think it is right now? Does it think it's being a helpful assistant, a tutor, a character in a story? How confident does it think it is? Is it in a mode where it's trying to please you? Those internal states plausibly shape its behavior just as much as its model of the user, maybe more. If you could surface even a rough version of that, it would be useful in a way that's very different from reading the text output, because the text is the polished end product and the internal state is closer to the actual machinery.

I think about it a bit like the instruments in a car. You don't need to understand the engine to benefit from a speedometer or a warning light. A good dashboard isn't a full readout of everything; it's a careful choice of a few things that matter and that people can act on. So the design challenge is twofold. On the science side, we need probes and features we actually trust, that are measuring what we think they're measuring, and that's still hard. On the design side, we need to figure out which of these self-representations are meaningful to an ordinary person and how to display them without creating false confidence or just overwhelming people.

There's also an interactive possibility that I find exciting. With the user model, we found you can sometimes not just read the representation but intervene on it, nudge it, and see the behavior change. With a self-model, you could imagine a user saying, "No, I don't want you to be in flattering mode right now, I want you to be critical," and having a control that does that at the level of the internal representation rather than just through the prompt. That gives people a kind of agency and transparency that I think will matter more and more as these systems become part of everyday life.

So I see it as part of a bigger shift: interpretability not just as a tool for researchers looking for bugs, but as something that ends up in the interface, for everyone.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that got us started down this path was a fairly simple observation. When you're talking to a chatbot, there's a lot going on inside the model that you can't see. And one of the things it seems to be tracking, at least in some implicit way, is a model of who it's talking to and a model of who it is. So the question we asked was: can we actually read that out, and if so, can we put it in front of the user in a way that's useful?

The analogy I like is the dashboard in a car. You don't need to understand how an engine works to drive, but you really want to know how fast you're going and whether you're about to run out of gas. Right now a chat interface gives you none of that. It's just a text box. So the idea of the dashboard is, alongside the conversation, you show a few key quantities about the model's internal state. In our first experiments we focused on the model's representation of the user, things like what age or gender or socioeconomic status it seems to have inferred. And it turns out you can find pretty clean linear probes for those, and the model's behavior actually changes depending on what it believes about you.

Now, the self-representation piece is the natural next step, and I think it may actually be more important. If the model has some internal notion of "what kind of entity am I right now," whether it's being, say, a helpful assistant versus playing a character, or whether it's in a mode where it's more likely to confabulate or to be sycophantic, that's exactly the kind of thing a user should be able to glance at. It's like a warning light. You wouldn't want to interrupt the conversation to explain the mechanism, but a little indicator that says "the model is currently operating in a mode where it's telling you what you want to hear" is enormously useful.

And there's a design challenge here that I find really interesting, because these representations are noisy, they're approximate, and you don't want to overstate what you know. So part of the work is figuring out how to show uncertainty honestly. But I think the broad vision is that the interface should give you some window into the model's beliefs, including its beliefs about itself, rather than treating the whole thing as a black box with a text input.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the useful thing would be to give people a sense of what the chatbot is doing and where its limits are. When you’re looking at a dashboard, you need to know things like: What data am I seeing? What’s missing? How much should I trust this conclusion? A chatbot could help explain those things, but only if it has some accurate representation of what it can access and what it has actually done.

Imagine asking, “Why did sales drop?” and having it say, “I checked these three regions, but I don’t have data for the fourth.” That gives you something concrete to investigate. And the dashboard could make that visible, so you’re not relying entirely on the chatbot’s account. To me, that’s an interesting design opportunity: connecting the conversation to evidence you can inspect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it becomes useful when it helps you understand what the system is doing. A dashboard usually gives you a view of some external process. With a chatbot, part of what you need to see is the chatbot itself: what information it has access to, what it’s assuming, and where it might need your help.

Imagine asking it to analyze a dataset. It could show you, “Here are the sources I’m using, here’s the filter I applied, and here’s something I couldn’t resolve.” That gives you places to intervene. You can say, “Actually, that’s the wrong source,” or, “You misunderstood that column.”

The tricky part is that a chatbot can give a very convincing account of itself without that account being accurate. So I’d want those representations tied to things we can actually observe and verify. Then the dashboard becomes a shared workspace where you can understand and steer the analysis.
